related_questions.question: What are the five warning signs of breast cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: Five common warning signs of breast cancer include: a new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes like dimpling or redness, nipple changes such as inversion or discharge, and breast pain. It's crucial to remember that these symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, but any new or concerning changes should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.
snippet_highlighted_words: a new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes like dimpling or redness, nipple changes such as inversion or discharge, and breast pain

list.title: New lump or thickening:
list.snippet: A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area is a common sign, but it's important to note that not all lumps are cancerous. Some are benign cysts or other non-cancerous conditions. However, any new lump should be checked by a doctor.

list.title: Changes in breast size or shape:
list.snippet: Noticeable changes in the size, shape, or contour of one or both breasts can be a warning sign. This could include a breast becoming larger or smaller, or developing an unusual shape.

list.title: Skin changes:
list.snippet: Changes in the skin of the breast, such as dimpling, redness, or thickening, can be a sign. Sometimes the skin may look like an orange peel. It's important to note that these changes can be harder to see on darker skin tones.

list.title: Nipple changes:
list.snippet: Nipple changes, such as an inverted nipple (turned inward), discharge (other than breast milk), or skin changes around the nipple, can be a warning sign. Any new or persistent nipple discharge, especially if it's bloody or occurs without breastfeeding, should be evaluated.

list.title: Breast pain:
list.snippet: While breast pain is common and often not related to cancer, persistent or localized pain in one area of the breast should be checked by a doctor, especially if it's not related to menstrual cycles or other known causes.

related_questions.question: What does stage 1 breast cancer feel like?

text_blocks.snippet: Stage 1 breast cancer may not cause noticeable symptoms, but when they do occur, they can include a new lump in the breast or underarm, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes like dimpling or redness, nipple discharge, or pain or tenderness. Many breast lumps are not cancerous, but any new or unusual changes should be checked by a doctor.
snippet_highlighted_words: a new lump in the breast or underarm, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes like dimpling or redness, nipple discharge, or pain or tenderness

list.snippet: Lump or thickening: A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area is a common early sign. Cancerous lumps often feel hard, have irregular edges, and may be painless, though some can be soft, round, or even painful.
Changes in breast size or shape: One breast may appear larger or misshapen compared to the other.
Skin changes: Dimpling, puckering, redness, or scaling of the breast skin can be a sign.
Nipple changes: Inversion (turning inward) or flattening of the nipple, or nipple discharge (including blood) can occur.
Pain: Some individuals may experience pain or tenderness in the breast or armpit, though this is not a common early symptom.
Swelling: Swelling of all or part of the breast, even without a lump, can be a symptom.
Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC): IBC is a rare, aggressive form that can cause breast swelling, redness, warmth, and a thickening of the skin, often without a lump.

list.title: Not all lumps are cancer:
list.snippet: Most breast lumps are benign (non-cancerous).

list.title: Early detection is key:
list.snippet: Finding breast cancer early, through screening or self-exams, increases the chances of successful treatment.

list.title: Consult a doctor:
list.snippet: Any new or unusual breast changes should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

list.title: Inflammatory breast cancer:
list.snippet: IBC can present with different symptoms and may not always be found with mammograms.

related_questions.question: Does breast cancer hurt when you push on it?

text_blocks.snippet: While most breast cancers don't cause pain, they can sometimes be felt as a hard, irregular lump that may be painful when pushed on, especially if the tumor is large or growing into surrounding tissue. However, breast pain is more commonly associated with other conditions like benign cysts or mastitis, according to the American Cancer Society.
snippet_highlighted_words: most breast cancers don't cause pain, they can sometimes be felt as a hard, irregular lump that may be painful when pushed on, especially if the tumor is large or growing into surrounding tissue

list.title: Breast Cancer Pain:
list.snippet: Although not a primary symptom for most breast cancers, some women with breast cancer may experience pain or discomfort in the breast, especially if the tumor is large or pressing on nerves.

list.title: Non-Cancerous Breast Conditions:
list.snippet: Painful lumps in the breast are more often caused by benign conditions like cysts or mastitis, which can cause inflammation and pain.

list.title: Breast Cancer Lumps:
list.snippet: Breast cancer lumps, when felt, are often described as hard, irregular, and painless, but can become painful as they grow or impinge on surrounding tissue.

list.title: Importance of Checking:
list.snippet: If you experience breast pain, it's crucial to get it checked by a doctor, especially if the pain persists or is accompanied by other symptoms like a lump, skin changes, or nipple discharge.

list.title: When to See a Doctor:
list.snippet: If you have breast pain that is severe, persistent, or accompanied by other symptoms like a lump, skin changes, or nipple discharge, the American Cancer Society recommends you should see a doctor to determine the cause.

text_blocks.snippet: The most common sign of breast cancer is a new lump or mass in the breast. Other signs include swelling, skin irritation or dimpling, breast or nipple pain, nipple retraction, and nipple discharge other than breast milk. Swelling in the underarm area can also be a sign, even before a lump is felt in the breast. It's crucial to see a healthcare provider for any new or concerning changes in the breast.

list.title: New lump or mass:
list.snippet: A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area is the most common sign.

list.title: Swelling:
list.snippet: Swelling of all or part of the breast, even without a lump, can indicate breast cancer.

list.title: Skin changes:
list.snippet: Irritation, dimpling, redness, scaliness, or thickening of the breast or nipple skin can be a sign.

list.title: Nipple changes:
list.snippet: Nipple retraction (turning inward), changes in the nipple's direction, or nipple discharge (other than breast milk) can be concerning.

list.title: Pain:
list.snippet: Breast or nipple pain can be a symptom, but it's also a common symptom of many other benign conditions.

list.title: Breast shrinking:
list.snippet: If one breast appears to shrink while the other does not, it could be due to a tumor around the chest wall, which pulls in the breast tissue.
Enlarged lymph nodes: Swelling or lumps in the underarm area can be a sign of breast cancer spreading to lymph nodes.
Changes in skin texture: Skin might appear like orange peel or feel different to the touch.
Pain in the shoulder or right side of the abdomen (secondary breast cancer): Pain in these areas can be a sign of breast cancer spreading to the liver.
Nausea, loss of appetite, and weight loss (secondary breast cancer): These can also be signs of breast cancer spreading to the liver.

list.title: Early detection is key:
list.snippet: Regular breast cancer screening is important because early-stage breast cancer may not cause noticeable symptoms.

list.title: Self-awareness:
list.snippet: Regular breast self-exams can help you become familiar with your breasts and notice any changes early.

list.title: See a doctor:
list.snippet: If you notice any new or concerning changes in your breasts, it's essential to see a healthcare professional for evaluation.
